paragraphs: Based on the opening of "The Most Dangerous Game," Sanger Rainsford is an unsympathetic and arrogant person who believes that strength gives him the right to dominate others without remorse. When Whitney suggests that hunted animals feel fear, Rainsford dismisses the idea immediately by asking, "Who cares how a jaguar feels?" This shows that he completely lacks empathy for living creatures and considers their suffering completely unimportant compared to his own enjoyment of the sport. Furthermore, Rainsford justifies this cold perspective when he tells Whitney, "The world is made up of two classes—the hunters and the huntees. Luckily, you and I are hunters." This quotation demonstrates his self-centered worldview, dividing everything into the strong and the weak while proudly placing himself above those who suffer. Through these remarks, Rainsford is characterized as a hardened, unfeeling realist who values power over compassion.

The story is The Most Dangerous Game. In the beginning, Rainsford is shown to be a cold and unsympathetic person who feels no pity for the animals he hunts. When Rainsford and Whitney talks on the yacht, Whitney tries to say that jaguars feel fear, Rainsford dismisses this idea completely. For example, he bluntly asks, "Who cares how a jaguar feels?" Because he believes animals do not have any feelings or understanding. This quote shows how heartless Rainsford is since he completely disregards the suffering of creatures just to enjoy his sport. Later in their conversation, he tells Whitney that "the world is made up of two classes—the hunters and the huntees," this statement displays his arrogant worldview. The hunters in his mind is naturally superior to everything else. A hunter like him never care about the prey, which proves that Rainsford only respects power and looks down on anything weaker than himself.

Based on the beginning of "The Most Dangerous Game," it is clear that Rainsford is a very callous person who completely lacks empathy for living creatures. When Whitney suggests that jaguars experience terror while being hunted, Rainsford quickly dismisses the idea and asks, "Who cares how a jaguar feels?" This quote proves that he does not care about what the jaguar feels because he asks who cares about the feelings of the animal. Because he tells Whitney to be a "realist," which means someone who makes realistic paintings of nature, so he believes that emotions are just useless things that soft people invent. Furthermore, Rainsford shows his cold mindset when he boldly explains to his friend, "The world is made up of two classes—the hunters and the huntees. Luckily, you and I are hunters." By dividing all existence into those who kill and those who get killed, Rainsford demonstrates that he feels entirely superior to prey, and later when he rests "indolently," which means he is acting furious and stressed, he shows how deeply he obsesses over dominating the natural world. Ultimately, Rainsford is portrayed as a selfish hunter who refuses to consider the suffering of anything he pursues.

This quote demonstrates that Rainsford strictly divides existence into the strong versus the weak, arrogantly assuming that being a predator places him safely above the fear and pain experienced by those at his mercy. Through these interactions, Rainsford is clearly established as a detached, unsympathetic hunter who feels entitled to dominate the natural world without remorse.

Overall, the opening dialogue shows that Rainsford is an unfeeling man who only cares about his own power.
